input:
Before the analogy is put to work, it is as well to be clear about the case in which it can be expected to fail, since an estimate that is used outside its range of validity is worse than no estimate at all. The Chilton-Colburn analogy asserts that the transfer processes correspond to one another in form, so that $j_D$ and $f$ are connected, and knowledge of the one can be used in place of a measurement of the other. The correspondence depends on the layer adjacent to the surface behaving in the same way for each process, and it is precisely this condition that is liable to break down in practice.

A numerical check shows the analogy being applied in the manner intended. For the flow that is being considered, $f$ has the value 0.03, and the relation $j_D = f/2$ then gives 0.015 for $j_D$, which is the figure that a measurement would be expected to approach if the analogy holds for this flow. The check is deliberately short: its purpose is to fix the form of the relation, not to validate the analogy itself, which no single substitution is capable of doing.

The case in which the analogy fails is the case in which the properties of the fluid are not effectively constant across the transfer layer. A strong variation of properties across the layer affects the transfer of momentum and the transfer of mass differently, and once that happens the correspondence between the processes, which is the entire content of the analogy, has been lost. The estimate may still be computed, and it will still return a number, but the number is no longer supported by the reasoning that produced the relation, and it should not be carried into a design calculation on the strength of the analogy alone.
target:
The qualification belongs at the front of the analogy, not after it. The Chilton-Colburn analogy asserts a correspondence of form between the transfer processes: $j_D$ follows $f$, and either quantity can stand in for the other. The correspondence rests on one condition, that the layer at the surface behaves in the same way for each process. Where that condition fails, the analogy fails with it, and the failure is silent: the arithmetic still returns a number.

The numerical check is short and fixes the form only. For the flow under consideration $f$ is 0.03, and the relation $j_D = f/2$ gives 0.015 for $j_D$. That is the value the analogy requires; a measurement near it supports the application, and a measurement far from it withdraws the support. The check validates nothing by itself, because substitution into a relation cannot test the relation, and a writer who presents the check as a test has claimed more than the arithmetic contains.

Properties that vary strongly across the transfer layer break the condition. Momentum and mass respond differently to the variation, and the correspondence that is the whole content of the analogy is gone. An estimate computed in that state of affairs has no basis in the analogy, whatever its numerical value, and a design calculation that takes it up takes up an unsupported figure. The analogy is used where its condition holds and set aside where the condition fails, and the distinction is made on the properties of the layer, not on the plausibility of the result. A plausible result from a broken correspondence is still an unsupported result, and it is the more dangerous for looking sound. The distinction matters most where the result is convenient, because a convenient number is the one least likely to be questioned before it is used.
